articles.description: Ahead of next month’s midterm US elections, Donald Trump has increasingly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging energy prices back home, which are causing the president political headaches. However, analysts say the main driver of higher fuel prices remains the US–Iran war. Which Russian sites have been targeted? Ukraine has intensified its drone attacks on Russia’s energy industry over the past 18 months, seeking to cut the Kremlin’s revenues and undermine its ability to finance the war. The strikes have targeted “mostly refineries”, Julien Mathonniere, an economist at Energy Intelligence, told AFP. On average, one Russian refinery was hit every three days during the first eight months of the year, according to the International Energy Agency. “Russia’s net diesel exports fell by approximately 80 per cent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, from around 1.05 million barrels per day to just 200,000 barrels per day,” said Viktor Kurilov, an analyst at Rystad Energy. In response to the disruption in domestic fuel supplies, Moscow introduced a ban on diesel exports from July until the end of October. Why does this concern Trump? Trump has repeatedly condemned the attacks on Russian refineries, saying Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky disobeyed his orders to halt the strikes. By contrast, Trump has not commented on the intensification in recent months of Russian strikes against Ukrainian territory, which have caused a surge in civilian casualties. Trump’s frustrations come as the Republicans face dim prospects in the November midterm elections, partly because of soaring fuel prices. US diesel prices at the pump climbed to a record of $6.53 per gallon at the end of September, up from $3.75 per gallon before the war, according to the American Automobile Association. Energy price rises are also fuelling inflation across the economy. What is the Mideast role? Ukraine’s strikes explain “about one-third of the global diesel shortfall, currently estimated at 1.7 to 1.8m barrels per day”, said Mathonniere. But “the impact of previous drone strikes (by Kyiv) on global product prices before the Middle East crisis was minimal”, James Henderson, a researcher at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, told AFP. Energy exports from the Gulf have plunged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran from February caused Tehran to respond by choking off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas transit. At the same time, maritime freight costs have soared and major refining capacity in the Middle East has been hit, adding to upward pressure on oil prices. Can prices fall before midterms? Relations between Kyiv and Washington soured further this month after Trump announced a controversial agreement with Moscow to lift certain sanctions and allow Russian diesel imports, supposedly to ease prices. The US president said Wednesday that he believed an end to the Russia-Ukraine war could be closer than ever, as the Kremlin said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month. For now, however, the strikes continue. “There’s not much that can be done in the very short term to lower diesel prices,” said Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad Energy. Even if the Russia conflict ended or an energy ceasefire was reached, the impact “wouldn’t really move the needle massively for the US midterm elections”, he added. Repairs to damaged infrastructure take time, while continued hostilities in the Middle East drive energy prices higher.

articles.title: West Bank attack wounds 5 Israelis as Netanyahu cancels events
articles.description: An attack in the occupied West Bank wounded at least five Israelis on Friday and triggered a shootout that left two Palestinians dead, prompting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to cancel political events days ahead of elections. An AFP journalist who witnessed the firefight saw two Palestinian men in casual attire and armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city of Hebron. The journalist reported that Israeli forces eventually shot and killed the attackers. The Israeli military said soldiers had rushed to the Judea Junction area, also known as the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint, after the early-morning shooting attack. “Israel Defence Forces (IDF) soldiers eliminated two terrorists and continue searches in the area,” it claimed in a statement. Netanyahu claimed Israel had prevented a “major attack” after soldiers killed the two armed Palestinians. He added that he had instructed the military to “impose a cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full closure of the entire West Bank starting today”. articles.title: R4 ministers' meeting expresses solidarity with Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
articles.description: At the Regional Four (R4) Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in Istanbul on Friday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and other foreign ministers expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia over the recent Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The R4 group, comprising Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, emerged in March and has been focusing on regional security and mediation efforts between the United States and Iran. The R-4-plus meeting with France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom is also being held in Istanbul. According to a statement by the FO on social media, DPM Dar participated in the sixth R4 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting alongside Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, and Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud of Saudi Arabia. The ministers reviewed developments in the region since their last meeting in New York in September, with “particular focus on the situation in the Middle East and related security challenges and conflicts”, the FO said. They expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their support for its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The FO added that the ministers also condemned the Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and underscored the importance of respecting state sovereignty. “They discussed ways to strengthen regional coordination and advance diplomatic efforts to promote lasting peace, security, and stability,” it said. Bilateral meetings Dar earlier held bilateral meetings with the Turkish and Egyptian foreign ministers, on the sidelines of the R-4 meeting and a meeting between the R-4 and European diplomats in Istanbul, the FO said. In a post on X, the FO said that Dar met with Fidan ahead of the ministerial meeting, thanking him for hosting the meetings. The pair discussed bilateral relations and regional developments, particularly the situation in the Middle East and Palestine. “They expressed concern over threats to regional stability and underscored the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and coordinated efforts to promote regional peace and security,” the FO statement said. Additionally, Dar and Fidan strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their commitment to close coordination on regional issues, including under the Makkah Defence Agreement. “Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship and brotherhood between Pakistan and Turkiye, and to deepening cooperation across all areas of mutual interest, both bilaterally and in multilateral fora,” the FO added. Later, the FO said that Dar also met with Egyptian FM Abdelatty on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting, where the two exchanged views on regional and international developments. In particular, they discussed the situation in Palestine and the Middle East, and underscored the importance of “sustained dialogue and diplomacy” in addressing challenges in the region. The two reaffirmed the “longstanding and fraternal ties” between Pakistan and Egypt, and highlighted the importance of sustained high-level engagement to further advance bilateral relations, the FO statement said. “They agreed to impart greater momentum to cooperation across a range of areas, including trade, business-to-business linkages, agriculture, pharmaceutical, connectivity, renewable energy, defence, and people-to-people exchanges,” the FO added. The ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to continued consultations and closer coordination under the R4 framework, as well as on matters of mutual interest, it said. Separately, DPM Dar met with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on the sidelines of the meeting and expressed the desire to further strengthen bilateral ties “through sustained engagement and cooperation across multiple areas of mutual interest”, the FO said. According to the FO, the two ministers discussed relations between Pakistan and Germany and exchanged views on regional and international developments. They stressed the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and sustained international engagement to promote peace and stability and to address the evolving challenges in the region. Dar “welcomed the constructive engagement” of Germany, France, Italy and the UK with the R4 framework, the FO said, adding that he underscored the value of “continued consultations and diplomatic coordination on issues of shared concern”. Arrival in Istanbul Dar left for Istanbul earlier in the day and is attending the meeting at the invitation of Fidan. In a post on X, the FO said that upon his arrival, Dar arrived in Istanbul and was received by Director General of the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs Cihad Erginay and Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires Shaiq Ahmed. The FO added that during his one-day visit, Deputy Prime Minister (DPM) Dar would participate in the R-4 and R-4-plus meetings with France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom. Dar would also call on Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts, it said. Earlier, the FO said that the ministers will participate in a meeting with counterparts from the European E-3 bloc — UK, France, and Germany — following the R-4 meeting. The E-3 group comprises three European powers that established the grouping more than 20 years ago to advance diplomatic coordination on Iran’s nuclear programme. Italy will also be a part of the meeting, the FO had added. “This will be the first meeting of the seven countries in this format,” the FO said. “The meetings will focus on key regional developments and explore coordinated diplomatic approaches to address shared challenges and advance regional peace and stability,” it added. DPM Dar is also set to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts during his visit as well. “Pakistan’s participation reflects its continued commitment to constructive diplomacy, regional cooperation and the peaceful resolution of disputes,” the FO said. Talks to revolve around Hormuz, Saudi Arabia British foreign minister Ed Miliband’s office said the talks would essentially revolve around “the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia”. It said Miliband “will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the (Hormuz) crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms”. He will also stress “how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilising the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab El-Mandeb and the Suez Canal”, it added. France confirmed the talks on “the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications”, hailing it as a first “in this format… against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region.” The meeting will aim to “strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all,” the French foreign ministry said. A Turkish diplomatic source also told Reuters a day earlier that the seven countries would meet in the R-4+E-3 format for the first time at Turkiye’s initiative as wars involving Iran , Yemen and Ukraine threaten shipping routes and regional security. Fidan is expected to emphasise the need for a diplomatic solution to the war between the United States and Iran, the importance of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, and reiterate Turkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security against attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed by Islamabad, Ankara, and Riyadh, the sources said. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

articles.title: 'Will petrol be available in December?': Senate echoes with shortage concerns even as minister says no supply issues
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The Senate echoed with fuel supply concerns on Friday as PPP’s Sherry Rehman questioned petrol availability for December and Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned of a bleak situation amid heightening Middle East tensions. The concerns were raised even after Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kayani said that there were no supply issues. He told the Senate during the question hour that more than 10 million people were benefiting from the government’s targeted fuel subsidy scheme, while Rs1,676 billion had been budgeted under the petroleum levy for the current year. The subsidy was being provided at petrol pumps, and there was no fuel supply problem, he said. Kayani added that the impact of regional conflict on petroleum prices was being felt across countries, but the government was providing targeted relief to motorcyclists, rickshaw and loader operators, and users of small cars. Last week, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb also said Pakistan had enough supplies to last through November. But what about December? asked PPP’s Rehman in the Senate on Friday. “What is the government’s plan for the availability of petroleum products? Will there be rationing? Members of Parliament have concerns whether petrol will be available till December,” she said. She demanded that the government brief Parliament on any rationing and contingency plans it may have been working on. Senator Rehman said reports of renewed attacks on Iran and escalating conflict in West Asia had added to uncertainty surrounding Pakistan’s petroleum supplies and had direct implications for the country’s energy security, economic stability and lives of ordinary citizens. Wondering if Pakistan would have adequate supplies under current circumstances, she said, “These are not minor concerns.” She warned that any disruption in the supply of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) would have a serious impact across the country, pointing out that Pakistan relied on imports for nearly 70 per cent of its LPG requirements while domestic production accounted for only 30pc. Pakistan received five LPG cargoes last year, whereas only two were expected this year, she said, demanding that a supply plan be presented to Parliament. Turning to the carbon levy, the PPP senator, who chairs the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, claimed the carbon levy on petroleum products was not being spent on environmental protection. “Yesterday, during the meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, the finance additional secretary acknowledged that the carbon levy is not being spent on environmental projects. A levy is not a tax; it goes straight into the Federal Consolidated Fund where there is no ring-fencing for spending on climate action,” she said. Rehman added that the revelation confirmed what was denied earlier during a Senate session. “The levy is being absorbed into general federal receipts instead of being earmarked for climate resilience despite severe and devastating floods facing all provinces,” she alleged. “The federal government continues to collect this revenue through the petroleum levy, and the money goes into the Federal Consolidated Fund; it cuts through all the provinces. There should not be a carbon levy in the next budget, unless it is restructured as a carbon tax that is ring-fenced for mitigation and climate action. There has to be accountability for every rupee collected.” “When an item is called a carbon levy, it is to be ring-fenced and then disbursed in consultation with the climate ministry,” she asserted. For his part, Senate Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned that a war engulfing key energy routes would worsen Pakistan’s energy crisis, as key maritime chokepoints come under threat. He linked the external crisis to domestic shortages, saying Punjab was already facing a flour shortage while the country was witnessing an LPG shortage. Meanwhile, politicians were ignoring real issues and were busy trying to “ conquer ” provinces, he said, seemingly referring to the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Oct 11. He also questioned the claims that terrorists were given shelter in Swat and asked how many had been caught. Meanwhile, police, who were the guarantors of peace, were being made to fight the public, he claimed. He also touched upon the conflict between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia, saying that Pakistan should mediate between the two sides. With Yemen’s civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure , including energy facilities and airports, in recent days. This, coupled with the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February, has resulted in the choking of key energy supply routes — the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and energy price hikes globally. Finance Minister Aurangzeb said during an interview last week that Pakistan had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices, but attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were “worrying” for the country’s longer-term economic outlook. He said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

articles.description: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised Pakistan’s “rising diplomatic profile in the resolution of regional and global disputes”, in a meeting with President Asif Ali Zardari in Berlin on Friday. President Zardari is currently on a three-day visit to Germany, having departed yesterday, as the two countries are set to mark the 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations. According to a statement posted by the president’s office, the two leaders also discussed challenges related to Afghanistan. President Zardari said that while Pakistan “has no conflict with the Afghan people”, it would not allow terrorists to use Afghan soil to attack Pakistan’s citizens and violate its sovereignty. Steinmeier appreciated Pakistan for facilitating the verification of 500 Afghans “destined to be repatriated to Germany”, it said, adding that he also commended Pakistan’s humanitarian assistance to “millions of Afghans” over more than four decades. He also took a “significant interest” in the Makkah defence pact, which has been signed between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia. In response, President Zardari said the pact was aimed at “ensuring regional security and provided a security alternative to regional conflicts, and it is not directed against any specific country”. The German president expressed hope that the two countries would continue to engage with reinforced efforts in the fields of business and trade to promote “bilateral business, education collaboration and technological cooperation”. For his part, President Zardari thanked Steinmeier for his invitation and the hospitality extended to him and his delegation. President Zardari further expressed his gratitude for Steinmeier’s acknowledgement of Pakistan’s “sincere mediation role” in the conflict between the United States and Iran, the statement said. He said Pakistan viewed the resolution of conflicts through the lens of sustained dialogue and constructive negotiations, “for the sake of regional as well as global peace and stability”. During the meeting, President Zardari also stressed the need to “realise the available potential for expanding existing political, economic and defence cooperation” between Pakistan and Germany, with “greater focus on economy and trade, emerging technologies, climate resilience, skills development, people-to-people and cultural exchanges”, the statement said. The president said that Pakistan “highly values” Germany as a major European partner, and expressed admiration for German support towards women’s empowerment, social protection and human development. Pakistan was prepared for expanding bilateral cooperation beyond traditional areas into “innovative and mutually beneficial collaboration” with Germany, in the areas of scientific development, healthcare and education, vocational training and technological advancement, trade and investment, agriculture, commerce and industry, and climate resilience, through enhanced government-to-government, business-to-business and expert-level interactions, the statement further quoted President Zardari as saying. He said the visit reflected Pakistan’s “commitment to deepening its longstanding cordial, friendly relations with Germany and readiness to translate existing relations into a stronger, robust and mutually beneficial partnership through sustained constructive engagement”. President Zardari invited the German president to Pakistan, who responded that he would consider a visit “at an appropriate time”. Both presidents participated in delegation-level talks after their one-on-one meeting, according to the statement. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and Sindh’s provincial ministers Sharjeel Memon and Jam Khan Shoro, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and Pakistan’s Ambassador to Germany Salman Sharif were part of the Pakistani delegation. Earlier, President Zardari was given a guard of honour upon his arrival at the German Ministry of Defence, with Steinmeier also present on the occasion, the statement added. In a statement issued on Thursday, the Foreign Office (FO) said the president’s visit, scheduled for Oct 22-24, is “part of high-level exchanges between Pakistan and Germany”. articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The Senate echoed with fuel supply concerns on Friday as PPP’s Sherry Rehman questioned petrol availability for December and Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned of a bleak situation amid heightening Middle East tensions. The concerns were raised even after Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kayani said that there were no supply issues. He told the Senate during the question hour that more than 10 million people were benefiting from the government’s targeted fuel subsidy scheme, while Rs1,676 billion had been budgeted under the petroleum levy for the current year. The subsidy was being provided at petrol pumps, and there was no fuel supply problem, he said. Kayani added that the impact of regional conflict on petroleum prices was being felt across countries, but the government was providing targeted relief to motorcyclists, rickshaw and loader operators, and users of small cars. Last week, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb also said Pakistan had enough supplies to last through November. But what about December? asked PPP’s Rehman in the Senate on Friday. “What is the government’s plan for the availability of petroleum products? Will there be rationing? Members of Parliament have concerns whether petrol will be available till December,” she said. She demanded that the government brief Parliament on any rationing and contingency plans it may have been working on. Senator Rehman said reports of renewed attacks on Iran and escalating conflict in West Asia had added to uncertainty surrounding Pakistan’s petroleum supplies and had direct implications for the country’s energy security, economic stability and lives of ordinary citizens. Wondering if Pakistan would have adequate supplies under current circumstances, she said, “These are not minor concerns.” She warned that any disruption in the supply of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) would have a serious impact across the country, pointing out that Pakistan relied on imports for nearly 70 per cent of its LPG requirements while domestic production accounted for only 30pc. Pakistan received five LPG cargoes last year, whereas only two were expected this year, she said, demanding that a supply plan be presented to Parliament. Turning to the carbon levy, the PPP senator, who chairs the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, claimed the carbon levy on petroleum products was not being spent on environmental protection. “Yesterday, during the meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, the finance additional secretary acknowledged that the carbon levy is not being spent on environmental projects. A levy is not a tax; it goes straight into the Federal Consolidated Fund where there is no ring-fencing for spending on climate action,” she said. Rehman added that the revelation confirmed what was denied earlier during a Senate session. “The levy is being absorbed into general federal receipts instead of being earmarked for climate resilience despite severe and devastating floods facing all provinces,” she alleged. “The federal government continues to collect this revenue through the petroleum levy, and the money goes into the Federal Consolidated Fund; it cuts through all the provinces. There should not be a carbon levy in the next budget, unless it is restructured as a carbon tax that is ring-fenced for mitigation and climate action. There has to be accountability for every rupee collected.” “When an item is called a carbon levy, it is to be ring-fenced and then disbursed in consultation with the climate ministry,” she asserted. For his part, Senate Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned that a war engulfing key energy routes would worsen Pakistan’s energy crisis, as key maritime chokepoints come under threat. He linked the external crisis to domestic shortages, saying Punjab was already facing a flour shortage while the country was witnessing an LPG shortage. Meanwhile, politicians were ignoring real issues and were busy trying to “ conquer ” provinces, he said, seemingly referring to the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Oct 11. He also questioned the claims that terrorists were given shelter in Swat and asked how many had been caught. Meanwhile, police, who were the guarantors of peace, were being made to fight the public, he claimed. He also touched upon the conflict between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia, saying that Pakistan should mediate between the two sides. With Yemen’s civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure , including energy facilities and airports, in recent days. This, coupled with the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February, has resulted in the choking of key energy supply routes — the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and energy price hikes globally. Finance Minister Aurangzeb said during an interview last week that Pakistan had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices, but attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were “worrying” for the country’s longer-term economic outlook. He said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

articles.title: AIPAC’s shift
articles.description: ON Wednesday, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) made an unusual announcement . The organisation would no longer endorse or make direct contributions to candidates running in US elections. This marks the end of a practice that AIPAC began in 2021 (its lobbying started in the ‘50s). This does not mean that the Israel lobby will stop trying to influence US elections. AIPAC will continue mobilising individual donors. However, the announcement is an acknowledgement of the growing difficulties associated with overt affiliation with the lobby and the pro-Israel agenda. The genocide in Gaza and the war in Iran have created a situation where many Americans are questioning their country’s support for Israel and the resources devoted to it. Democratic candidates have challenged US involvement in the Middle East and the $3.8 billion in annual assistance Washington provides Israel. No campaign has illustrated this with greater clarity than that of Dr Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the US Senate seat in Michigan. In the Democratic primary, AIPAC spent $30 million backing El-Sayed’s opponent, Haley Stevens. Other political action committees also spent heavily on her campaign. In contrast, El-Sayed spent only $3.2m, most of it raised from individual donors. Despite all this, El-Sayed won. One reason was his willingness to confront Stevens over AIPAC’s involvement in the race and to question why US taxpayer money should go to another country. What El-Sayed was able to do is connect two different realities of the American political context. First, he tapped into the American fatigue with interminable wars in the Middle East. Again, and again, he argued that the US had “no business” becoming embroiled in further conflicts, while infrastructure and institutions at home were decaying. His criticism of Donald Trump’s escapades in Iran became part of this argument. Second, El-Sayed connected the affordability crisis facing Americans to questions about government spending and the country’s relationship with Israel. Americans struggling to afford healthcare and basic groceries are naturally questioning how public money is spent abroad. War-weary Americans can see through Israeli machinations. El-Sayed is not campaigning on Israel alone. Affordability and healthcare are central issues for him, and he supports a government-funded Medicare For All option that would make healthcare accessible to millions of people. His own background in public health makes him a persuasive speaker on these issues. AIPAC’s affiliated Super PAC has now directed spending against El-Sayed in his contest with Republican Mike Rogers. This is a departure from AIPAC’s usual support for Democratic candidates in Michigan. American Zionists and the well-heeled donors behind AIPAC may see the Michigan contest not simply as an electoral battle in a US state but also as an indicator of how anti-Israel sentiment is becoming increasingly pervasive among the Democratic electorate. The announcement that there will be no more overt endorsements reflects the liability that public association with AIPAC can create for some candidates. It is a sea change in the character of Democratic politics in the US. There are global implications in this shift. If El-Sayed wins — and one hopes he does despite the millions that AIPAC is now pouring into his opponent’s coffers — it will mean that other Democratic lawmakers in the House and Senate will have to think twice about voting to send billions of dollars to Israel. In the past, Democratic politicians have voted en masse for just these sorts of measures. Israel is very proud of its genocidal actions in Gaza. It is also quite smug about having persua­d­­ed Trump to at­­tack Iran. It sees both of these act­ions and its continuing excesses in Gaza and the West Bank as victories. This, however, is an illusion. The reality is that in the process of achieving the former, Israelis forgot that ordinary, war-weary Americans can see through its machinations. This is important not because Israel cares what Americans think but because Israel is entirely dependent on the US, receiving almost 70 per cent of its military equipment from them. As the election of Zohran Mamdani in New York City and the hopeful rise of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan show, Americans are signalling just how fed up they are with Israel’s intrusions in their own government and its attempts to create dual loyalties in their political leadership. As American leaders stop signing blank cheques for Israel as in the past five decades, Israel is likely to face enormous struggles. Already an isolated nation, increasingly detested by the world for the carnage of innocents, its future is not that of a victorious nation but of a widely reviled one. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

articles.title: Israel launches major West Bank operation after soldiers killed
articles.description: Israel’s military launched an operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday, which it said would last several days and include searches and building demolitions, after gunmen killed two soldiers days ahead of Israeli elections in which security has been a key focus. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight race to keep his job in Tuesday’s vote, having campaigned on promises to keep Israelis safe , and he and his right-wing allies visited the scene of the attack to pledge an even harder line on West Bank militancy. Security forces were searching targets and questioning Palestinians to “locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure” in the Hebron area from where they said the attackers had emerged, according to a joint statement from the Israeli military and Shin Bet domestic security agency. Israeli forces were also “demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat at the site of the encounter”, they said, adding that “counterterrorism operations” were underway at dozens of locations. The operation “is expected to continue for several days,” the statement, released late on Friday, said. Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised Friday’s fatal attack on two Israeli soldiers as a “heroic operation” and called on supporters to carry out more. A Hebron-based AFP photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between the soldiers and two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle. Israeli forces eventually shot dead the attackers. Netanyahu credited the soldiers with having “prevented what could have been a major attack”, and ordered a lockdown in the West Bank. Visiting Hebron, the premier said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were “considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since” the 1967 war. The first step would see Israeli forces “enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure,” he claimed. The military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, he said, the scene of a large-scale operation launched in January 2025 that the United Nations said forcibly displaced thousands. Israeli rights group B’Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from pursuing “plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through a spokesman, voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides. ‘Exactly like Gaza’ Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank “ exactly like in Gaza ”. National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based “Palestinian Authority must be dismantled”. No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority — which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank — was connected to Friday’s attack. Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are especially vocal supporters of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government but are illegal under international law. Israel vowed to obliterate the group in the wake of the October 7, 2023 attack . Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the upcoming vote, said he was praying for soldiers wounded in Friday’s shooting. The operation comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters. According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023. Israeli figures show that at least 51 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

articles.title: Trump’s threat to strike Iran raises public concerns, congressional questions
articles.description: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump has renewed his threat of military action against Iran, raising questions about public support for the war and Congress’s ability to restrain further escalation . With midterm elections approaching on November 3, polls show widespread dissatisfaction with the war , particularly over rising fuel prices and the risk to American troops. Reports of renewed US-Israeli military planning have also raised concerns about possible strikes after the elections. Trump made his latest threat at a rally in Florida on Friday. “We may do another little Epic Fury ,” he said, referring to the US military operation against Iran. He gave no details about when another operation might begin. The remarks followed an ABC News report on Thursday that the US military and the Israel Defence Forces had drawn up options for renewed joint strikes. The report cited two Israeli sources familiar with the plans, who said the strikes would most likely take place after the midterms. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly, however, told ABC News that “the United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” The reports indicate that further military action is being considered, but they do not establish that Trump has ordered an attack. Negotiations remain another possibility. Strategic choices and political pressure In an analysis published on October 23, James M. Lindsay, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, outlined three options for Trump: escalate the conflict, negotiate with Tehran or maintain the current position. “All three options have substantial downsides and a questionable likelihood of succeeding,” Lindsay wrote. Further attacks could increase pressure on Iran but might prolong the conflict without securing a political settlement. Negotiations would require the two sides to bridge their differences, while maintaining the current position could leave the conflict unresolved. Andrew Payne, research director for Europe, Russia and the Americas at Chatham House, argued in an October 15 analysis that foreign policy could play an unusual role in this year’s midterm elections. The war’s economic consequences could influence voters who might otherwise focus primarily on domestic issues, particularly the cost of living. Public opinion turns against the war A Pew Research Centre survey conducted from September 28 to October 4 among 5,062 US adults found that 65 per cent disapproved of Trump’s handling of the military action against Iran, while 33pc approved. The survey also found that 73pc were extremely or very concerned about higher fuel prices, and 71pc about American troops being wounded or killed. Nearly half, 47pc, expected the military action to continue for more than another year. A separate Associated Press -NORC poll published on October 22 found that roughly seven in 10 registered voters wanted the next Congress to make ending the Iran war a top priority. About eight in 10 gave similar priority to reducing the cost of living. The poll surveyed 1,119 US adults from October 8 to 12. The findings point to pressure on the administration to address the war’s duration and economic consequences. However, dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the conflict does not necessarily mean that voters would oppose every possible military operation. Can Congress restrain Trump? Congress can scrutinise military operations, hold oversight hearings and use its control over federal spending to influence the course of the war. Lawmakers can also invoke the War Powers Resolution to challenge military action. The resolution requires the president to notify Congress in certain circumstances when US forces enter hostilities. It also establishes procedures for lawmakers to consider whether military action should continue. Funding could become particularly important if the conflict expands. Congress can approve, restrict or condition spending for military operations, potentially increasing the political cost of a prolonged campaign. The extent of congressional pressure would depend partly on whether Republicans remain united behind Trump. If some Republican lawmakers join Democrats in challenging the war, the administration could face greater scrutiny of its objectives and plans for ending the conflict. Even a congressional challenge, however, would not automatically prevent the president from ordering another strike. The question after November 3 The immediate question is whether Trump will maintain his stated position against attacking Iran before the midterms. The larger issue is whether the election results will alter the political constraints on his decisions. The reported military planning and Trump’s latest remarks keep the prospect of renewed strikes alive, but neither establishes that an attack has been scheduled. A change in control of either chamber of Congress could affect oversight and funding debates, although it would not automatically prevent further military action. Whether the combined pressures of public dissatisfaction, economic concerns and congressional scrutiny lead Trump towards negotiations or renewed strikes remains unclear.

articles.title: As Israeli election looms, Trump advisers see opportunity beyond Netanyahu
articles.description: President Trump has endorsed Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday's Israeli election, but some of his advisers see opportunity for his Middle East agenda in a government led by someone else, U.S. officials tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump has never worked with an Israeli prime minister other than Netanyahu, and doesn't personally know any of the other candidates. The two have forged a close but often turbulent relationship. "He's the devil he knows," one Trump adviser said, describing the president's view of Netanyahu. Driving the news: After weeks of hesitation, Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday — and even suggested his defeat would have consequences for U.S.-Israel relations. One U.S. official described the endorsement as a win-win for Trump, regardless of the outcome. If Netanyahu wins — or remains in power as caretaker prime minister — Trump could claim credit for rescuing him politically and use that leverage to press for concessions. If Netanyahu loses and his opponents form a government, Israel's new leaders would still have every incentive to cultivate good relations with Trump. His endorsement of their rival would quickly become a footnote. Behind the scenes: Many of Trump's closest advisers opposed his decision to endorse Netanyahu, believing the president should stay out of the Israeli election, according to sources familiar with the discussions. Vice President Vance notably declined to follow Trump's lead when asked about the election this week, amid growing hostility toward Netanyahu in parts of the MAGA movement. "I'm not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I'm not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu. I think the president's endorsement is ultimately what matters," Vance told reporters. Zoom in: Vance, who endorsed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán days before his election defeat in April , said he would no longer get involved in foreign elections. The vice president is among the senior Trump officials who became disillusioned with Netanyahu during the war with Iran, according to sources familiar with their thinking. Vance and other top aides believe Netanyahu's pre-war assessments to the White House were mistaken, deepening questions about whether he remains the best partner for achieving Trump's regional ambitions. The big picture: Once the Israeli election and U.S. midterms are over, Trump will face a defining choice for his Middle East agenda: whether to join Netanyahu in another major military operation against Iran. Netanyahu is eager to move forward. But the election results could influence Trump's decision, or at least the timing of any renewed large-scale fighting. Trump also wants to move beyond the Iran war and pursue an ambitious diplomatic agenda that includes implementing his Gaza peace plan , brokering deals between Israel and Lebanon and Syria , and ultimately securing a historic Israeli-Saudi peace agreement . Whether Trump can make progress on those goals will depend in part on who governs Israel — and what kind of coalition emerges from Tuesday's vote. The intrigue: Behind the scenes over the last six months, several of Trump's top advisers have grown dissatisfied with Netanyahu on key regional priorities. Gaza: Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have expressed frustration with Netanyahu's reluctance to advance implementation of the president's peace plan. Syria: Trump's envoy Tom Barrack has similar concerns about the Netanyahu government's approach to Damascus and continued Israeli military operations in Syria. Lebanon and the West Bank: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his team have a better relationship with Netanyahu, but believe Israel could do more to strengthen Lebanon's government. They are also frustrated by Netanyahu's failure to do more to curb settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. Between the lines: Some U.S. officials say a new Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners could be easier to work with. White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly declined to comment, referring Axios to Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu on Truth Social . State of play: Three major Israeli television networks released their final pre-election polls Friday, all showing Netanyahu's coalition falling well short of a parliamentary majority. All three projected just 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc in the 120-member Knesset — 17 fewer than his current coalition holds. His Likud party, which currently holds 32 seats, was projected to win just 20. The polls gave former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc between 52 and 56 seats, with another 14 to 16 going to two Arab Israeli parties. Channel 11 also projected four seats for a reservists party unaffiliated with either bloc. Pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 was the major outlier, projecting 60 seats for his bloc and 30 for Likud in a poll earlier this week. What to watch: The polls point to a potential political deadlock: Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot appears to have a clear path to the 61 seats needed to form a government. Eisenkot would need to bring Arab Israeli parties into his coalition, which he has ruled out, or form a minority government with their outside support — an arrangement some of his potential partners oppose. A unity government between Netanyahu and his rivals is considered highly unlikely. If neither side can assemble a governing majority, Israel could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining in power as caretaker prime minister. The bottom line: Rather than ushering in a new government more receptive to Trump's agenda, Tuesday's election could leave the president dealing with a weakened Netanyahu and an Israeli political system consumed by another prolonged crisis.

articles.title: Israeli forces displace families in occupied West Bank's Hebron after 2 soldiers killed
articles.description: Israeli forces pushed into the occupied West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday and displaced around 250 families, some in the middle of the night, vowing to exact a heavy price for a deadly attack on soldiers . The Palestinian Authority called for international pressure on Israel to protect residents, who said soldiers announced the evacuations over loudspeakers late at night as they packed what they could and left. Days before tight elections , Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967, after Palestinian fighters killed two Israeli soldiers on Friday at a checkpoint. In the Hebron neighbourhood of Ein Deir Baha, nestled between two hills, vacated buildings were marked by X’s and the streets were deserted, save a pair of Israeli military vehicles. Israeli flags were draped on a house on the slope apparently taken over by troops. Higazi Shawer al-Tamimi, 70, a shopkeeper who sells live chickens and feed and plays a leadership role in the neighbourhood, said he was awakened at 1:00am by soldiers and a senior officer who said he had to leave. “I asked them how long the evacuation would last. They said: ‘Until further notice.’” He told AFP he had only a short time to pack, adding that for some residents, getting out of the neighbourhood was an ordeal. “For example, my wife’s mother, who is 90 years old and lives in the area, had to be carried out because she is ill,” he said. Visiting Hebron, Netanyahu said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were “considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since” the 1967 war. The first step would see Israeli forces “enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure”, he claimed. Hamas, while not claiming credit, hailed Friday’s attack on soldiers and called on supporters to carry out more. ‘Why should I be displaced?’ To Tamimi, this is only happening because Netanyahu wants to win the election on “the blood of the Palestinian people”. He said people were not going anywhere. “I have lived through all the stages of the occupation, and I will die here.” The Palestinian Authority said it was mobilising its diplomats to seek “urgent international action that goes beyond condemnation” to prevent forced displacement. Tamimi’s brother, Khaled Shawer al-Tamimi, 68, was staying with his son after the evacuation order. “The army was announcing through loudspeakers: ‘Leave the area.’ So we left.” He told AFP he was surprised to hear Friday’s assailants came from the neighbourhood, which he described as middle-class and law-abiding. “We have never seen or even heard a single gunshot being fired,” he said from his son’s sitting room as children flitted about. “Why should I be displaced from my house?” he continued. The attackers “are the ones who carried out the act, and if the Israeli government wants to punish them, it can punish them.” Israeli forces have already demolished some buildings in the immediate vicinity of where the attack took place, and the Tamimis said they did not know if their homes would meet the same fate. Hebron governor Khaled Dudin told AFP the army started in the attackers’ neighbourhood, “but there is no guarantee that the operation will not expand”, calling it a form of “collective punishment”. The governor said 150 families had been affected, while Hebron mayor Youssef al-Jaabari and local activist Issa Amro put the figure at 250. Israeli rights group B’Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from pursuing “plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through a spokesman, voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides. Netanyahu promises PA ‘surprise’ The Israeli military said it was “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” focused on the area of the two gunmen, who were both killed in a firefight. It added that the operation would last several days. But Netanyahu suggested that bigger action was coming. Asked if he agreed with the idea of dismantling the Palestinian Authority, as has been suggested by his far-right national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir, Netanyahu referred to Israeli military operations in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran. “We transformed the Middle East,” he said, repeating a common campaign refrain, in an interview with i24News . “There is a very big surprise for the Palestinian Authority as well.” There is no evidence that the Palestinian Authority had any involvement in Friday’s attack. Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank “ exactly like in Gaza ”. Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are especially vocal supporters of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government but are illegal under international law. Netanyahu has linked the assailants to Hamas, the resistance group in Gaza that carried out the Oct 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest in Israel’s history. The attack came amid rising tensions in the West Bank as Israeli settlers, who enjoy strong support from Netanyahu’s far-right allies, ramp up seizures of Palestinian land and attacks. Rights group Yesh Din reported 672 incidents of settler violence over the past 26 days, nearly half related to the annual olive harvest. According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023. Israeli figures show that at least 51 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period. Polls show Netanyahu is neck and neck with an opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right former military chief who also opposes a Palestinian state but has promised to crack down on settler violence.

articles.title: Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperilling Republicans in midterms
articles.description: Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters choices. But this time, with Donald Trump’s war on Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a presidents approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue. As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperilling their control of Congress. A flag supporting US President Donald Trump outside the venue of his rally ahead of the midterm elections, in Macon, Georgia, the US on Oct 24, 2026. — Reuters Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78 per cent of Americans blame Trump’s policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings. Not since 2006, when then-president George W Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leaders handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome. The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago. The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies, said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Centre think tank in Washington. Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this. Politics driving foreign policy With Trump’s approval ratings touching historic lows , he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living. That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections. Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine. He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago. Firefighters work at the site of an office building damaged during a Russian jet drone strike in Kharkiv, Ukraine on Oct 23, 2026. — Reuters At the same time, he has promised not to order any new attack on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections. Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. Iran says its nuclear programme is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development programme in 2003. Some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine. For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the diplomatic stalemate, senior Iranian officials have told Reuters. Defending the administration’s approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: “President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear.” It’s the economy, stupid Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House. And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns — it’s the economy, stupid, as the Clinton-era adage goes — dominate voters’ choices. Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs. Footage released by IRIB and attributed to the IRGC shows oil tanker Gem No 2 ablaze, in this screengrab obtained from a video released on Oct 10, 2026. — Reuters/File Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions. Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the limits of US power have been increasingly exposed, analysts say. Legislative balance of power in play Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to gain control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play. For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term. But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on Nov 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit. Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase — when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made. “For many presidents who feel politically constrained [at home], foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington. Analysts say Trump’s handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way — or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

articles.title: Dar orders urgent action to rein in rising wheat prices
articles.description: • Calls for increased market supply, warns against hoarding and speculation • PTI Kisan Wing welcomes wheat support price, seeks effective procurement mechanism ISLAMABAD: Expressing concern over rising wheat prices, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday directed federal and provincial governments to take all necessary measures, including increasing market supply, to bring prices under control. Chairing a cabinet committee meeting to review the stocks, prices and supply of essential commodities, Mr Dar emphasised that safeguarding national food security and ensuring the availability of essential items at reasonable prices were government priorities. The participants reviewed national reserves, procurement frameworks, domestic consumption and price trends. They were informed that stocks of essential commodities remained adequate, ensuring stability in local supplies. The committee was briefed that domestic and imported wheat stocks were sufficient to meet requirements until the next harvest. Regarding sugar, the committee was informed that its price in the domestic market remained well below the targeted retail price of Rs155 per kg, with surplus stocks available until the next crushing season. Mr Dar directed federal and provincial authorities to closely monitor market networks, stressing that all organisations must show zero tolerance for hoarding and market speculation. The meeting was attended by National Food Security and Research Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain, Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tariq Bajwa, the secretaries of the national food security and research and commerce ministries, the chief secretaries of all provinces, and senior officials from relevant federal and provincial departments. Implementation urged In a related development, the PTI Kisan Wing has welcomed the government’s announcement of a wheat support price of Rs4,500 per maund (40kg), while expressing reservations about its implementation and demanding concrete measures to ensure farmers receive the announced rate for their produce. A day earlier, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif set the new indicative wheat support price for 2027, increasing it by Rs1,000 from the rate fixed last year. According to a statement issued on Saturday, PTI Kisan Wing Central Secretary Information Khalid Nawaz Sadhraich said the announcement had come after a prolonged wait and persistent demands by farmers’ organisations, which had repeatedly urged the government to protect growers from rising production costs and financial losses. He welcomed the announcement but said its significance would depend on whether the government ensured its implementation in letter and spirit. Merely announcing a support price would serve little purpose if farmers continued to be denied the promised rate when selling their wheat, he added. Referring to previous wheat procurement seasons, Mr Sadhraich said farmers had repeatedly suffered despite government claims and official announcements regarding support prices. “In the absence of an effective procurement mechanism, middlemen and commission agents exploited growers’ vulnerability, compelling them to sell their produce at throwaway prices, often without effective intervention by the relevant authorities,” he said. He cautioned the government against repeating these mistakes, saying farmers could not afford another season of financial uncertainty after investing heavily in seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, diesel, electricity and irrigation. “A support price announced on paper provides no meaningful relief unless farmers can actually sell their wheat at the declared rate,” he added. Mr Sadhraich demanded that the government immediately announce a clear wheat procurement policy, ensuring that it purchased wheat directly from farmers at the announced rate. He said the policy should spell out procurement arrangements and operational procedures and establish an effective monitoring mechanism to prevent exploitation by middlemen and ensure that the benefits reached genuine growers. He also called for the timely establishment of procurement centres, transparent purchasing procedures and an accessible complaints mechanism so that small and medium-sized farmers could sell their produce without unnecessary hurdles or pressure from market intermediaries. articles.title: Prudent warning
articles.description: AS speculation grows regarding fresh US-Israeli aggression against Iran, major Muslim states of the wider Middle East, as well as European powers, have clearly expressed their lack of appetite for any such misadventure. Meeting in Istanbul on Friday under the ‘R4+E3’ umbrella, the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkiye, the UK, Germany, and France discussed several global hotspots, including Iran and Ukraine. Italy also participated in the meeting. The Turkish foreign minister said that “no one supports” military intervention in Iran at this moment, while France’s top diplomat said any escalation “would only have losers”, besides increasing oil prices, which are already high. There is good reason for the international community to be worried. Strong signals are emerging from Tel Aviv and Washington that the US and Israel are planning a new assault on Iran, reportedly after the American midterms on Nov 3 — perhaps even earlier. US President Donald Trump has himself said that “we may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the name America gave to the aggression launched in February. While the US leader is known for his bluster and often non-serious threats, in this regard he may actually mean what he has said. The US has been sending more troops and military equipment to the Middle East, and American and Israeli forces have reportedly rehearsed attack plans. Tel Aviv is particularly enthused about going after Iran again. Doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results each time is equated with folly. But arrogance has blinded both the US and Israel to this reality. Israel had first attacked Iran in October 2024, while both the US and the Zionist state initiated two more aggressive operations against the Islamic Republic, in June 2025 and February 2026. These attacks, particularly the assault launched this year, inflicted huge damage on Iran, decimating its military, political, and religious leadership. But the country regrouped, defended itself, and fought back against the aggressors. The Iranians have reaffirmed that any new attack will be met with “offensive” measures. All of this is cause for alarm. The Gulf states that host American facilities will again be in the line of fire, which is why Muslim countries have warned against a new conflict. But will the war lobbies in Washington and Tel Aviv listen? Many governments and most people of the Middle East are tired of war, and want to rebuild their lives and economies. If conflict and bloodshed return, the shockwaves caused by disrupted energy and trade flows will leave few economies unscathed. Therefore, America should abandon its plans to further destabilise the region. Instead, it should rein in its ally Israel and its bloodthirsty leaders. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

articles.title: 'Never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting': Obama unloads on Trump ahead of US midterms
articles.description: US President Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday one of his Democratic predecessors did just that. Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations . Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration. Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the November 3 vote as a “circuit breaker” to “at least rein in some of the foolishness” of Trump’s presidency. “We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government,” Obama said. Obama, president from 2009 until Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative. The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats’ frequently repeated criticisms of Trump and of Republicans’ willingness to go along with him. “We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this,” Obama said. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favours like this … Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A Reuters /Ipsos poll in August found that 63 per cent of Americans think the president and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69pc believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings. Obama also ridiculed the administration’s claims of victory against Iran . He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters. “Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world,” Obama said. The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasising unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth someone “laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops” and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said.

The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington “may do another little Epic Fury,” referring to the US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28. “Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same,” said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran. “They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past.” An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz , a key route for global energy supplies. These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks. Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation — moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region. In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports. In June, Iran agreed with the United States to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding , laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it. Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict. “The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same,” said Araghchi. “To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces.”
